paragraphs: Yajnavalkya was a great sage. In India the scriptures advised that a man should renounce the world in old age, so one day he told his wife Maitreyi that he was leaving, and that all his money and belongings were now hers.

Maitreyi did not reach for the gift. Instead she asked: if the whole earth were filled with wealth and it all belonged to her, would it make her immortal? No, said Yajnavalkya; she would be rich, nothing more. Then what should she do to gain immortality? If he knew, she wanted to be told. Her husband was deeply touched. She had always been dear to him, he said, and this question made her dearer still. He asked her to sit, listen, and then meditate on what he would say.

His teaching was startling. A wife does not love her husband for the husband's sake, he said, but for the sake of the Self within. The same goes for love of children, wealth, the world and even the gods: all of it is really love of the Atman. That Self, therefore, must be heard about, reasoned about and meditated upon, and once It is known, everything is known.

Swamiji explained what this means. The selfish love we see in the world is only a tiny shadow of a vast love for the Self that is the whole universe. When we love something as a separate little object, cut off from the whole, that love ends in grief. When we see the beloved as the Atman itself, love becomes perfect and free. Those who love without knowing the Self are selfish; those who know It are sages.

Yajnavalkya used everyday images. You cannot catch the sound of a drum, conch or vina from afar, but take hold of the instrument and you master the sound. Just as a lump of salt dissolves into the sea, all things rise from and return to this one infinite Being. Maitreyi grew afraid: would there be no one left to love? The sage reassured her that where there is duality, one sees and knows another; but when all has become the Self, who is left to see whom?

He ended by describing how the earth, air, sun, moon and lightning are all "sweet" to every being, and every being sweet to them, because the same shining, immortal One lives in all of it and in us. Swamiji added that good and evil are only that One showing more or less clearly. To meditate on this unity, he said, was exactly what Yajnavalkya was teaching Maitreyi.
learn: Maitreyi chose understanding over an inheritance, a bold choice at any age. The story also suggests a healthier way to love: not by clutching people as possessions, but by seeing the same deep worth in them that lives in you.
